summary: Your implementation correctly finds a valid pair on typical cases and passed all visible tests, but it missed a hidden case consistent with the problem’s large-input constraint. The main issue is using an O(n^2) nested-loop approach while also incorrectly claiming O(n), which is a key expectation for this prompt.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed, but 1 hidden test failed, consistent with a performance/time-limit issue on large inputs.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Returned correct indices for the visible suite and handled the no-solution fallback by returning an empty list (even though the prompt guarantees exactly one valid answer). The loop bounds (j starts at i+1) avoid using the same element twice.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Meet the stated constraints: the hidden failure indicates the solution does not complete within limits on the largest case. Replace the pairwise scan with the canonical hash-map complement check to ensure correctness under time constraints.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You quickly identified a straightforward approach and implemented it cleanly without needing hints. You also considered an input guard (even if unnecessary given constraints).
dimensions.what_to_improve: When constraints explicitly warn about O(n^2), treat that as a requirement to pivot to a different strategy (here: “seen map / complement lookup”). Build a habit of selecting the approach starting from constraints rather than from the simplest implementation.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You gave a clear, high-level description of what the code does (scan remaining elements for the complement).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Complexity explanation was incorrect: nested loops imply O(n^2). In future, explicitly account for the total number of inner-loop iterations (e.g., ~n(n-1)/2) and tie that back to constraint-driven feasibility.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: Your implementation uses O(1) auxiliary space, which is optimal for the brute-force family of solutions.
dimensions.what_to_improve: The expected optimal solution is O(n) time using a hash map of value -> index; your code stayed at O(n^2) despite constraints and also mischaracterized the runtime as O(n). Practice recognizing when space-for-time tradeoffs are required and be ready to justify them.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is simple, readable, and has clear control flow. Early return once a pair is found is good.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Align implementation with problem guarantees and expectations: remove unnecessary empty-input handling if the platform guarantees length >= 2, and implement the hash-map approach to match required performance.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You produced a working brute-force solution without hints and got all visible tests passing quickly.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independence here is limited by not independently incorporating the constraint warning into your approach selection. Practice self-checking: if the prompt flags O(n^2) as too slow, proactively switch to the known O(n) pattern rather than concluding the first solution is optimal.

thinking_and_logic: You implemented a brute-force nested scan: for each index i, you search j>i until you find nums[i] + nums[j] == target and return the pair. That approach is logically correct for finding a pair, and your j loop starting at i+1 prevents reusing the same element. However, it performs ~n(n-1)/2 checks in the worst case, which conflicts with the constraint note that O(n^2) will time out on the largest hidden case.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s brute_force approach (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space). The canonical optimal solution for this prompt is a single pass with a hash map (seen value -> index) where you compute complement = target - nums[i], check if it’s already seen, and return immediately; this achieves O(n) time and passes large hidden performance tests. Your solution did not adopt that pattern, and the incorrect O(n) complexity claim suggests a gap in runtime reasoning.

next_steps.action: Re-implement Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (seen value -> index, check complement before insert).
next_steps.why: This is the canonical optimal approach in the answer key and is required to satisfy the time-limit constraints on large inputs.
next_steps.how: Maintain dict seen = {}; iterate i, x in enumerate(nums): if target-x in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; else seen[x] = i.

next_steps.action: Practice complexity accounting for nested loops and common pitfalls (e.g., summations).
next_steps.why: You stated O(n) for an O(n^2) algorithm; correcting this will improve both solution selection and interview communication.
next_steps.how: For each loop, write the number of iterations: outer n, inner ~n-i-1; sum over i to get n(n-1)/2. Do this explicitly before claiming a bound.

next_steps.action: Do 5–10 “constraint-driven” drills where you must choose between brute force vs hash map vs sorting/two-pointers.
next_steps.why: To build the reflex of pivoting when constraints rule out a naive approach (as in this prompt).
next_steps.how: Examples: Two Sum variants, subarray sum equals K, longest consecutive sequence, pair difference, and 'sorted array' two-sum with two pointers.

patterns_to_study: Single-pass hash map for complement lookup (Two Sum pattern)
encouragement: You’re very close—your core logic is fine; the main upgrade is adopting the standard hash-map pattern and tightening up complexity reasoning so your solution matches the constraints and your explanation matches the actual runtime.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
